To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
single post-exposure treatment with CDV, even if initiated at late stage of disease, is sufficient to rescue animals from lethal ECTV challenge.

(1) single post-exposure treatment with cidofovir can protect mice from lethal ectromelia virus infection; (2) cidofovir efficacy is independent of the time of treatment initiation; (3) cidofovirexposure does not impair the immune response following vaccinia virus immunization; (4) cidofovin and vaccinia virus immunizations do not provide any additional protection; (5) the efficacy of cidofovir is dose dependent.
(a) A single CDV treatment at 100 mg/Kg is sufficient to rescue animals from lethal ECTV infection even when initiated on day 6 post-exposure (i.e. 4 days prior to death).
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a treatment strategy for orthopoxviral infections, in particular for smallpox, which is based on the use of antivirals in conjunction with vaccination, and which can be used in the event of a bioterrorist attack.
a novel treatment approach that could potentially be used in the first days post smallpox exposure, when vaccination is not effective.

the possibility of a single post-exposure treatment with CDV as a stand-alone therapy for human smallpovirus disease, and in combination with vaccination for the treatment of human monkeypox disease, in the case of a reemergence of either of these diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CDV treatment can be used to rescue animals at different stages of disease, but that the best time for treatment is within 2–4 days p.e..
a single CDV treatment can rescue animals from ECTV infection, regardless of the time of initiation, provided that the dose is sufficiently high.
the efficacy of CDV treatment is dependent on the initiation time of treatment and dose, but also on the immune status of the animal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a single dose of 100 mg CDV/kg body weight, given at 1 day p.e., can rescue animals from a lethal orthopox infection.

the efficacy of CDV is dose dependent, yet even a low dose of CDV (5 mg/Kg) is able to rescue animals at a time point when untreated animals are already showing clinical symptoms of disease (day 6 p.e.).
CDV is a potent drug for the treatment of orthopoxviruses and that it can be used in combination with vaccination to achieve protection against lethal infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CDV treatment can be used to rescue animals at progressive stages (even 6 days p.e.) of lethal disease.

a single CDV treatment, given at different doses, is efficacious for rescuing animals at progressive stages p.e. and that the treatment window is wide enough to allow for the administration of the drug even when vaccination is not feasible.
a single dose of CDV, administered as early as one day p.e., can protect mice from lethal infection, and that the efficacy of this treatment does not rely on the immune status of the animals.
